modern_osis:
Proverbs — Separate book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Henry explains the purpose of Proverbs by expanding the opening verses of the book.

First, these are the proverbs of Solomon, David's son and king of Israel.

Second, they concern knowledge of wisdom, devotion toward God, moral instruction and discipline, and understanding counsel that is wise and prudent.

Third, they teach how to acquire practical wisdom. True wisdom becomes visible in the way a person lives, especially in righteous conduct toward other human beings.

Fourth, they give simple people discernment through sound principles and a correct understanding of good and evil. They give the young knowledge so they need not go wrong through ignorance, and discretion through considering God's commands so they need not go wrong through stubbornness.

Henry contrasts this teaching with proverbs from other nations, many of which he says are grounded in selfishness, cunning, pride, injustice, national contempt and hostility.

Solomon's proverbs instead rest upon godliness, charity, justice, benevolence and genuine prudence.

Their complete moral purity, Henry concludes, shows that they are the word of God.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe use of the Proverbs.1–6Exhortations to fear God and obey parents.7–9To avoid the enticings of sinners.10–19The address of Wisdom to sinners.20–33
Why these proverbs teach us (verses 1–6)

The lessons in Proverbs are straightforward and will greatly benefit people who recognize how little they know and how much they need to be taught.

Young people who govern their lives by these instructions will grow in both understanding and discretion.

Solomon teaches the most important truths. But one greater than Solomon speaks here.

Christ speaks through his word and Spirit.

He is the Word and the Wisdom of God, and he himself has become wisdom for us.

Reverence for God and instruction from parents (verses 7–9)

Fools are people who possess no real wisdom and follow whatever schemes they invent, disregarding both reason and reverence for God.

Children are rational creatures.

When we explain what they should do, we ought also to explain why.

Yet children are fallen and often stubborn, so instruction must be accompanied by rules and authority.

Let us consider God's truths and commandments worthy of the highest honor.

If we truly treasure them, their excellence will be evident in our lives.

Refusing to follow sinners (verses 10–19)

Wicked people eagerly invite others onto paths leading to destruction.

Sinners like company in their sins, and for that reason their responsibility becomes even greater.

Young people should be exceedingly careful.

Do not consent.

Do not speak as they speak, act as they act or do what they want you to do.

Do not share in their wrongdoing.

How terrible that someone could enjoy another person's destruction!

They prize worldly wealth as though it were something truly substantial or precious.

But many thousands have ruined themselves by valuing the world's riches too highly.

Sinners imagine that wrongdoing will benefit them.

The path of sin, however, runs downhill and soon escapes their control.

Those who want to avoid destruction in this life and the next must refuse even the first step onto that path.

Greed drives people into practices that shorten their lives and harm others.

What would a person gain by acquiring the entire world while losing life—and how much worse to lose the soul?

Wisdom calls sinners to repentance (verses 20–33)

Solomon has shown the danger of listening to Satan's temptations.

He now shows how dangerous it is to refuse God's invitation.

Christ himself is Wisdom.

He addresses three groups.

First, the simple: people content with shallow ideas of good and evil, prejudiced against the Lord's ways, who flatter themselves about their sins.

Second, mockers: proud people who laugh at everything holy and turn sincere religion into a joke.

Third, fools: those who positively hate being instructed and have become deeply hostile to godliness.

The command is plain: Turn when Wisdom rebukes you.

We have not responded rightly to rebuke unless we turn from evil to good.

God gives extraordinary encouragement.

No one can accomplish sincere conversion through personal strength, but he promises: I will pour out my Spirit to you.

Conversion requires special grace, and that grace will not be refused to those who seek it.

Christ's love and promises should make us listen carefully even when he rebukes us.

How long do sinners expect to remain safe on such a dangerous path, knowing how uncertain life is and what it means to die without Christ?

They may now feel secure and dismiss every warning.

But calamity will come.

Now God offers to hear their prayers; those who persist in rejecting him may later cry out too late.

Are we still despising Wisdom?

Let us listen diligently and obey the Lord Jesus, finding peace of conscience, confidence in God and deliverance from evil in life, death and eternity.
classic_reading:
[Prov.1.1-Prov.1.6]
Proverbs
The subject of this book may be thus stated by an enlargement on the opening verses. 1. The Proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel. 2. Which treat of the knowledge of wisdom, of piety towards God, of instruction and moral discipline, of the understanding wise and prudent counsels. 3. Which treat of the attainment of instruction in wisdom, which wisdom is to be shown in the conduct of life, and consists in righteousness with regard to our fellow-creatures. 4. Which treat of the giving to the simple sagacity to discover what is right, by supplying them with just principles, and correct views of virtue and vice; and to the young man knowledge, so that he need not err through ignorance; and discretion, so that by pondering well these precepts, he may not err through obstinacy. Take the proverbs of other nations, and we shall find great numbers founded upon selfishness, cunning, pride, injustice, national contempt, and animosities. The principles of the Proverbs of Solomon are piety, charity, justice, benevolence, and true prudence. Their universal purity proves that they are the word of God.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The use of the Proverbs. | (1-6) |
Exhortations to fear God and obey parents. | (7-9) |
To avoid the enticings of sinners. | (10-19) |
The address of Wisdom to sinners. | (20-33) |
Verses 1-6
The lessons here given are plain, and likely to benefit those who feel their own ignorance, and their need to be taught. If young people take heed to their ways, according to Solomon's Proverbs, they will gain knowledge and discretion. Solomon speaks of the most important points of truth, and a greater than Solomon is here. Christ speaks by his word and by his Spirit. Christ is the Word and the Wisdom of God, and he is made to us wisdom.
[Prov.1.7-Prov.1.9]
Verses 7-9
Fools are persons who have no true wisdom, who follow their own devices, without regard to reason, or reverence for God. Children are reasonable creatures, and when we tell them what they must do, we must tell them why. But they are corrupt and wilful, therefore with the instruction there is need of a law. Let Divine truths and commands be to us most honourable; let us value them, and then they shall be so to us.
[Prov.1.10-Prov.1.19]
Verses 10-19
Wicked people are zealous in seducing others into the paths of the destroyer: sinners love company in sin. But they have so much the more to answer for. How cautious young people should be! "Consent thou not." Do not say as they say, nor do as they do, or would have thee to do; have no fellowship with them. Who could think that it should be a pleasure to one man to destroy another! See their idea of worldly wealth; but it is neither substance, nor precious. It is the ruinous mistake of thousands, that they overvalue the wealth of this world. Men promise themselves in vain that sin will turn to their advantage. The way of sin is down-hill; men cannot stop themselves. Would young people shun temporal and eternal ruin, let them refuse to take one step in these destructive paths. Men's greediness of gain hurries them upon practices which will not suffer them or others to live out half their days. What is a man profited, though he gain the world, if he lose his life? much less if he lose his soul?
[Prov.1.20-Prov.1.33]
Verses 20-33
Solomon, having showed how dangerous it is to hearken to the temptations of Satan, here declares how dangerous it is not to hearken to the calls of God. Christ himself is Wisdom, is Wisdoms. Three sorts of persons are here called by Him: 1. Simple ones. Sinners are fond of their simple notions of good and evil, their simple prejudices against the ways of God, and flatter themselves in their wickedness. 2. Scorners. Proud, jovial people, that make a jest of every thing. Scoffers at religion, that run down every thing sacred and serious. 3. Fools. Those are the worst of fools that hate to be taught, and have a rooted dislike to serious godliness. The precept is plain; Turn you at my reproof. We do not make a right use of reproofs, if we do not turn from evil to that which is good. The promises are very encouraging. Men cannot turn by any power of their own; but God answers, Behold, I will pour out my Spirit unto you. Special grace is needful to sincere conversion. But that grace shall never be denied to any who seek it. The love of Christ, and the promises mingled with his reproofs, surely should have the attention of every one. It may well be asked, how long men mean to proceed in such a perilous path, when the uncertainty of life and the consequences of dying without Christ are considered? Now sinners live at ease, and set sorrow at defiance; but their calamity will come. Now God is ready to hear their prayers; but then they shall cry in vain. Are we yet despisers of wisdom? Let us hearken diligently, and obey the Lord Jesus, that we may enjoy peace of conscience and confidence in God; be free from evil, in life, in death, and for ever.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPromises to those who seek wisdom.1–9The advantages of wisdom.10–22
Seeking the wisdom God freely gives (verses 1–9)

Those who earnestly seek wisdom from heaven will never regret the effort they have made.

The gift is free, but that does not remove the need for diligence in seeking it (John 6:27).

Those who seek will find; those who ask will receive.

Who receives this blessing?

The righteous, upon whom God's image is renewed, an image that includes true righteousness.

When we depend upon God and seek wisdom from him, he will enable us to walk in the paths of justice.

Wisdom protects the heart and conduct (verses 10–22)

Those who are truly wise avoid evil company and evil practices.

When wisdom governs us, it does not merely fill the mind with information.

It enters the heart.

It protects against both the corruption already within us and temptation arriving from outside.

Sin's ways are dark, unsafe and joyless.

How foolish to leave the bright and peaceful paths of uprightness for such roads!

Some people delight in both committing sin and watching others sin.

A wise person avoids their company.

He also avoids people who encourage lustful actions that defile the body, the living temple, and fight against the soul.

These are dangers that distress godly people and give thoughtful parents reason to be concerned for their children.

The suffering of others should serve as a warning.

Our Lord Jesus warned against sinful pleasures by speaking of the everlasting torments that follow them.

People caught in these traps rarely free themselves easily.

Sin's deceit hardens the heart and blinds the understanding.

Henry notes that many readers also understand these warnings figuratively, applying them to idolatry or to making the soul a servant of the body by pursuing forbidden objects.

The righteous and wicked alike will eventually leave this earth.

But the earth serves very different purposes for them.

For an unrepentant sinner, it is all the heaven that person will ever possess.

For the righteous, it is a place to prepare for heaven.

Does it not matter to us whether we share the wicked person's end or the everlasting joys promised to believers?
classic_reading:
[Prov.2.1-Prov.2.9]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Promises to those who seek wisdom. | (1-9) |
The advantages of wisdom. | (10-22) |
Verses 1-9
Those who earnestly seek heavenly wisdom, will never complain that they have lost their labour; and the freeness of the gift does not do away the necessity of our diligence, [John.6.27] Joh 6:27 Let them seek, and they shall find it; let them ask, and it shall be given them. Observe who are thus favoured. They are the righteous, on whom the image of God is renewed, which consists in righteousness. If we depend upon God, and seek to him for wisdom, he will enable us to keep the paths of judgment.
[Prov.2.10-Prov.2.22]
Verses 10-22
If we are truly wise, we shall be careful to avoid all evil company and evil practices. When wisdom has dominion over us, then it not only fills the head, but enters into the heart, and will preserve, both against corruptions within and temptations without. The ways of sin are ways of darkness, uncomfortable and unsafe: what fools are those who leave the plain, pleasant, lightsome paths of uprightness, to walk in such ways! They take pleasure in sin; both in committing it, and in seeing others commit it. Every wise man will shun such company. True wisdom will also preserve from those who lead to fleshly lusts, which defile the body, that living temple, and war against the soul. These are evils which excite the sorrow of every serious mind, and cause every reflecting parent to look upon his children with anxiety, lest they should be entangled in such fatal snares. Let the sufferings of others be our warnings. Our Lord Jesus deters from sinful pleasures, by the everlasting torments which follow them. It is very rare that any who are caught in this snare of the devil, recover themselves; so much is the heart hardened, and the mind blinded, by the deceitfulness of this sin. Many think that this caution, besides the literal sense, is to be understood as a caution against idolatry, and subjecting the soul to the body, by seeking any forbidden object. The righteous must leave the earth as well as the wicked; but the earth is a very different thing to them. To the wicked it is all the heaven they ever shall have; to the righteous it is the place of preparation for heaven. And is it all one to us, whether we share with the wicked in the miseries of their latter end, or share those everlasting joys that shall crown believers?

Trust the Lord rather than your own understanding (verses 1–6)

The life of believing obedience generally brings peace and health.

Even if it does not lengthen our earthly days, we will live forever in heaven.

Hold tightly to mercy and truth: God's mercy in making promises and his faithfulness in keeping them.

Walk consistently with both, treasure them and receive their comfort.

Trust in the Lord with your whole heart, believing that he is willing, wise and able to do what is best.

Those who know themselves find their own understanding a broken reed that cannot bear their weight.

Do not make plans that violate God's law.

Ask him to direct you even when a decision seems obvious.

In pleasant and successful circumstances, acknowledge him with thanks.

When a road is difficult and hedged in by thorns, acknowledge him with submission.

God will direct your paths, making them safe and ultimately good.

Honoring God and learning from fatherly correction (verses 7–12)

Few things are more destructive to reverence for God than conceit about our own wisdom.

The prudence and moderation religion teaches benefit both soul and body.

Earthly wealth is poor and perishable, but even that should be used to honor God.

Those who do good with what they have can be entrusted with more opportunities to do good.

When the Lord sends sickness and hardship, remember that he addresses us as his children.

Do not lose courage under a prolonged trial, surrender to despair or use sinful methods to seek relief.

A loving father corrects a child because he loves the child and wants that child to become wise and good.

Through grace, affliction may actually increase the holiness of God's people.

Wisdom more valuable than treasure (verses 13–20)

No jewel or earthly treasure compares with true wisdom, whether we consider this life or eternity.

Make obtaining wisdom your serious pursuit, willing to give up everything for it.

This Wisdom is Jesus Christ and the salvation he gives, received through faith and prayer.

Our unbelief, remaining sin and carelessness often lead us away from his pleasant paths, causing our own sorrow.

Christ is the Wisdom through whom the worlds were created and by whom they continue to exist.

Happy are those to whom God has made him their wisdom.

He possesses everything needed to fulfill his promises.

Wisdom guards our steps (verses 21–26)

Do not let Christ's words slip away from your attention.

Keep sound wisdom and discretion.

When we follow the Lord, his providence guards our natural life and his grace preserves our spiritual life.

He can keep us from falling into sin or being crushed by trouble.

Acting justly and avoiding unnecessary conflict (verses 27–35)

Our duty is to obey Christ's commands and follow his example.

Act justly, love mercy and beware of greed.

Be ready for every good work.

Avoid quarrels that serve no purpose.

When possible, it is better to bear a wrong patiently than to engage in pointless legal disputes.

Little lasting good comes from needless fighting.

Do not envy oppressive people who enjoy prosperity.

A disciple of Christ should not imitate their methods.

Greedy and self-indulgent people may mock such teaching, but their portion is everlasting contempt.

God favors the humble believer.

To piety, and to improve afflictions. | (7-12) |
To gain wisdom. | (13-20) |
Guidance of Wisdom. | (21-26) |
The wicked and the upright. | (27-35) |
Verses 1-6
In the way of believing obedience to God's commandments health and peace may commonly be enjoyed; and though our days may not be long upon earth, we shall live for ever in heaven. Let not mercy and truth forsake thee; God's mercy in promising, and his truth in performing: live up to them, keep up thine interest in them, and take the comfort of them. We must trust in the Lord with all our hearts, believing he is able and wise to do what is best. Those who know themselves, find their own understandings a broken reed, which, if they lean upon, will fail. Do not design any thing but what is lawful, and beg God to direct thee in every case, though it may seem quite plain. In all our ways that prove pleasant, in which we gain our point, we must acknowledge God with thankfulness. In all our ways that prove uncomfortable, and that are hedged up with thorns, we must acknowledge him with submission. It is promised, He shall direct thy paths; so that thy way shall be safe and good, and happy at last.
[Prov.3.7-Prov.3.12]
Verses 7-12
There is not a greater enemy to the fear of the Lord in the heart, than self-conceit of our own wisdom. The prudence and sobriety which religion teaches, tend not only to the health of the soul, but to the health of the body. Worldly wealth is but poor substance, yet, such as it is, we must honour God with it; and those that do good with what they have, shall have more to do more good with. Should the Lord visit us with trials and sickness, let us not forget that the exhortation speaks to us as to children, for our good. We must not faint under an affliction, be it ever so heavy and long, not be driven to despair, or use wrong means for relief. The father corrects the son whom he loves, because he loves him, and desires that he may be wise and good. Afflictions are so far from doing God's children any hurt, that, by the grace of God, they promote their holiness.
[Prov.3.13-Prov.3.20]
Verses 13-20
No precious jewels or earthly treasures are worthy to be compared with true wisdom, whether the concerns of time or eternity be considered. We must make wisdom our business; we must venture all in it, and be willing to part with all for it. This Wisdom is the Lord Jesus Christ and his salvation, sought and obtained by faith and prayer. Were it not for unbelief, remaining sinfulness, and carelessness, we should find all our ways pleasantness, and our paths peace, for his are so; but we too often step aside from them, to our own hurt and grief. Christ is that Wisdom, by whom the worlds were made, and still are in being; happy are those to whom he is made of God wisdom. He has wherewithal to make good all his promises.
[Prov.3.21-Prov.3.26]
Verses 21-26
Let us not suffer Christ's words to depart from us, but keep sound wisdom and discretion; then shall we walk safely in his ways. The natural life, and all that belongs to it, shall be under the protection of God's providence; the spiritual life, and all its interests, under the protection of his grace, so that we shall be kept from falling into sin or trouble.
[Prov.3.27-Prov.3.35]
Verses 27-35
Our business is to observe the precepts of Christ, and to copy his example; to do justice, to love mercy, and to beware of covetousness; to be ready for every good work, avoiding needless strife, and bearing evils, if possible, rather than seeking redress by law. It will be found there is little got by striving. Let us not envy prosperous oppressors; far be it from the disciples of Christ to choose any of their ways. These truths may be despised by the covetous and luxurious, but everlasting contempt will be the portion of such scorners, while Divine favour is shown to the humble believer.

Receiving the instruction of wisdom (verses 1–13)

We should regard faithful teachers as fathers and welcome their instruction, even when it includes correction and rebuke.

Solomon's parents instructed him because they loved him.

Wise and godly people in every age and social position agree that true wisdom is expressed through obedience and joined to real happiness.

Seek that wisdom diligently.

Especially seek mastery over the sinful desires within your own heart.

Work harder to obtain this spiritual wisdom than to acquire worldly riches.

Nothing is more necessary than a saving share in Christ.

A soul without wisdom and grace is spiritually dead.

How pitiful to possess wealth, status and power but die without understanding, without Christ, without hope and without God!

Listen to the One who has the words of eternal life.

Hold firmly to his instruction.

Then your path will be clear, and you can avoid being trapped or stumbling.

Avoiding evil paths and guarding the heart (verses 14–27)

The path of wicked people can appear pleasant or like the quickest way to accomplish something.

But it is evil and will end in harm.

If you love God and care for your soul, stay far away.

Do not simply try to keep an adequate distance from temptation.

Go as far from it as you can.

The path of the righteous is light, for Christ is both their Way and their Light.

They will not become perfectly holy until heaven, but there they will shine like the sun.

The path of sin is darkness.

Wicked people stumble without knowing why, and often do not reflect on why God has brought hardship upon them or what the outcome may be.

Listening attentively to Scripture is evidence that grace has begun working in the heart and a means through which that work grows.

God's word contains the right remedy for every disease of the soul.

Guard your heart with all diligence.

Protect it from doing harm and being harmed, because life flows from the heart.

Above all, ask the Lord Jesus for living water—the Holy Spirit who sanctifies and gives life that lasts forever.

Then you can put away corrupt speech and dishonest lips.

Turn your eyes away from empty attractions and look straight ahead.

Follow the rule of God's word and walk in the footsteps of the Lord and Master.

Lord, forgive our past sins and help us follow you more faithfully in the future.

[Prov.4.1-Prov.4.13]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Exhortation to the study of wisdom. | (1-13) |
Cautions against bad company, Exhortation to faith and holiness. | (14-27) |
Verses 1-13
We must look upon our teachers as our fathers: though instruction carry in it reproof and correction, bid it welcome. Solomon's parents loved him, therefore taught him. Wise and godly men, in every age of the world, and rank in society, agree that true wisdom consists in obedience, and is united to happiness. Get wisdom, take pains for it. Get the rule over thy corruptions; take more pains to get this than the wealth of this world. An interest in Christ's salvation is necessary. This wisdom is the one thing needful. A soul without true wisdom and grace is a dead soul. How poor, contemptible, and wretched are those, who, with all their wealth and power, die without getting understanding, without Christ, without hope, and without God! Let us give heed to the sayings of Him who has the words of eternal life. Thus our path will be plain before us: by taking, and keeping fast hold of instruction, we shall avoid being straitened or stumbling.
[Prov.4.14-Prov.4.27]
Verses 14-27
The way of evil men may seem pleasant, and the nearest way to compass some end; but it is an evil way, and will end ill; if thou love thy God and thy soul, avoid it. It is not said, Keep at a due distance, but at a great distance; never think you can get far enough from it. The way of the righteous is light; Christ is their Way, and he is the Light. The saints will not be perfect till they reach heaven, but there they shall shine as the sun in his strength. The way of sin is as darkness. The way of the wicked is dark, therefore dangerous; they fall into sin, but know not how to avoid it. They fall into trouble, but never seek to know wherefore God contends with them, nor what will be in the end of it. This is the way we are bid to shun. Attentive hearing the word of God, is a good sign of a work of grace begun in the heart, and a good means of carrying it on. There is in the word of God a proper remedy for all diseases of the soul. Keep thy heart with all diligence. We must set a strict guard upon our souls; keep our hearts from doing hurt, and getting hurt. A good reason is given; because out of it are the issues of life. Above all, we should seek from the Lord Jesus that living water, the sanctifying Spirit, issuing forth unto everlasting life. Thus we shall be enabled to put away a froward mouth and perverse lips; our eyes will be turned from beholding vanity, looking straight forward, and walking by the rule of God's word, treading in the steps of our Lord and Master. Lord, forgive the past, and enable us to follow thee more closely for the time to come.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesExhortations to wisdom. The evils of licentiousness.1–14Remedies against licentiousness, The miserable end of the wicked.15–23
Keep far from sexual temptation (verses 1–14)

Solomon warns young men, whom he addresses as his children, to refuse lustful desires.

Some readers understand the adulterous woman as a picture of idolatry or false doctrine, because both corrupt beliefs and conduct. But the passage's direct subject is sin against the seventh commandment.

Sexual wrongdoing has also repeatedly become a means by which Satan draws people from the worship of God into false religion.

Consider its terrible consequences. Sin's fruit is bitter, whichever aspect we consider. It wounds the person who follows it and leads to the torments of hell.

Its natural tendency is to destroy both body and soul.

We should therefore avoid not only the act itself but also everything that might lead to it.

Those who wish to avoid harm should keep away from danger.

If we deliberately put ourselves into temptation and then pray, Lead us not into temptation, we mock God.

Such sin damages reputation, wastes time, consumes property, destroys health and fills the mind with horror.

A person may feel merry now, but sooner or later sorrow will follow.

Someone convinced of sin's guilt blames personal folly rather than inventing excuses.

Repeated acts of sin become entrenched habits.

Through an extraordinary act of divine mercy, true repentance can prevent the final ruin of such a sinner.

But Henry warns that this is uncommon; many people die as they have lived.

What words could express the misery of a person who has destroyed himself and enters eternity tormented by an accusing conscience?

God's provision of marriage and his knowledge of all our ways (verses 15–23)

Lawful marriage is a God-appointed means of avoiding destructive sexual sins.

Yet marriage is not lived rightly unless the spouses attend to God's word, seek his direction and blessing, and act with genuine affection toward one another.

Always remember that hidden sins may escape human notice, but our ways are before the Lord.

He not only sees our conduct; he examines every step.

Those who foolishly choose a path of sin may justly be left by God to follow their own choices until those choices bring destruction.
classic_reading:
[Prov.5.1-Prov.5.14]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Exhortations to wisdom. The evils of licentiousness. | (1-14) |
Remedies against licentiousness, The miserable end of the wicked. | (15-23) |
Verses 1-14
Solomon cautions all young men, as his children, to abstain from fleshly lusts. Some, by the adulterous woman, here understand idolatry, false doctrine, which tends to lead astray men's minds and manners; but the direct view is to warn against seventh-commandment sins. Often these have been, and still are, Satan's method of drawing men from the worship of God into false religion. Consider how fatal the consequences; how bitter the fruit! Take it any way, it wounds. It leads to the torments of hell. The direct tendency of this sin is to the destruction of body and soul. We must carefully avoid every thing which may be a step towards it. Those who would be kept from harm, must keep out of harm's way. If we thrust ourselves into temptation we mock God when we pray, Lead us not into temptation. How many mischiefs attend this sin! It blasts the reputation; it wastes time; it ruins the estate; it is destructive to health; it will fill the mind with horror. Though thou art merry now, yet sooner or later it will bring sorrow. The convinced sinner reproaches himself, and makes no excuse for his folly. By the frequent acts of sin, the habits of it become rooted and confirmed. By a miracle of mercy true repentance may prevent the dreadful consequences of such sins; but this is not often; far more die as they have lived. What can express the case of the self-ruined sinner in the eternal world, enduring the remorse of his conscience!
[Prov.5.15-Prov.5.23]
Verses 15-23
Lawful marriage is a means God has appointed to keep from these destructive vices. But we are not properly united, except as we attend to God's word, seeking his direction and blessing, and acting with affection. Ever remember, that though secret sins may escape the eyes of our fellow-creatures, yet a man's ways are before the eyes of the Lord, who not only sees, but ponders all his goings. Those who are so foolish as to choose the way of sin, are justly left of God to themselves, to go on in the way to destruction.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesCautions against rash suretiship.1–5A rebuke to slothfulness.6–11Seven things hateful to God.12–19Exhortations to walk according to God's commandments.20–35
Beware of careless financial guarantees (verses 1–5)

Living according to God's word benefits us even in the present life.

We are stewards, not absolute owners, of our possessions. We will answer to the Lord for how we use them.

It is wrong to waste them through rash projects or agreements that may entangle us in difficulty and temptations.

No one should promise to pay another person's debt unless the amount is something they are able and willing to pay, without depriving their own family of what it needs.

When we guarantee a debt, we should consider it our own obligation.

If such care is necessary to escape debts owed to other people, how much more earnestly should we seek release from our debt before God!

Humble yourself before him. Seek Christ as your Friend and Advocate, and pray earnestly for forgiveness of sin and deliverance from destruction.

Learn diligence from the ant (verses 6–11)

Diligence in our work is both wise and right.

Its main purpose is not simply to become wealthy, but to avoid burdening others or bringing disgrace upon God's church.

Ants show more industry than lazy people. We can learn from even the smallest creatures and be ashamed by their example.

Habits of idleness and excessive self-indulgence grow stronger through repetition.

A wasted life leads toward poverty. At first poverty seems distant, like a traveler slowly approaching. When it arrives, it becomes like an armed man whom the careless person cannot resist.

The same warning applies to the soul.

How many people delight in the sleep of sin and dream of worldly happiness!

We should seek to wake them. We must also be diligent concerning our own salvation.

Turn away from the things God hates (verses 12–19)

If people who do nothing useful deserve rebuke, those who devote themselves to doing as much evil as possible deserve still stronger condemnation.

The wicked person described here plans speech and conduct cunningly and deliberately.

Destruction can overtake such a person suddenly and without remedy.

The passage lists seven things God hates.

Sins that destroy the peace and well-being of other people are particularly offensive to him.

We must learn to hate these sins in ourselves. Merely condemning them in other people accomplishes nothing.

Avoid such conduct; remain watchful and pray against it.

Show clear disapproval of those who practice it, whatever their rank or position.

Walk in God's commandments (verses 20–35)

God's word has something to teach us in every circumstance of life.

We should never resent faithful correction.

The repeated warnings against adultery are necessary because the sin is widespread and deeply evil.

Its consequences are destructive, and it can ruin the soul's spiritual life.

Notice how this chapter brings together its warnings.

Remember the One who willingly became our Surety—Christ—while we were strangers and enemies.

With such promises, motives and an example before us, how could Christians remain idle or careless?

Will we neglect the things pleasing to God and worthy of the gracious reward he promises?

We must guard every sense through which sinful influence can enter our thoughts and affections.

We are stewards of our worldly substance, and have to answer to the Lord for our disposal of it; to waste it in rash schemes, or such plans as may entangle us in difficulties and temptations, is wrong. A man ought never to be surety for more than he is able and willing to pay, and can afford to pay, without wronging his family; he ought to look upon every sum he is engaged for, as his own debt. If we must take all this care to get our debts to men forgiven, much more to obtain forgiveness with God. Humble thyself to him, make sure of Christ as thy Friend, to plead for thee; pray earnestly that thy sins may be pardoned, and that thou mayest be kept from going down to the pit.
[Prov.6.6-Prov.6.11]
Verses 6-11
Diligence in business is every man's wisdom and duty; not so much that he may attain worldly wealth, as that he may not be a burden to others, or a scandal to the church. The ants are more diligent than slothful men. We may learn wisdom from the meanest insects, and be shamed by them. Habits of indolence and indulgence grow upon people. Thus life runs to waste; and poverty, though at first at a distance, gradually draws near, like a traveller; and when it arrives, is like an armed man, too strong to be resisted. All this may be applied to the concerns of our souls. How many love their sleep of sin, and their dreams of worldly happiness! Shall we not seek to awaken such? Shall we not give diligence to secure our own salvation?
[Prov.6.12-Prov.6.19]
Verses 12-19
If the slothful are to be condemned, who do nothing, much more those that do all the ill they can. Observe how such a man is described. He says and does every thing artfully, and with design. His ruin shall come without warning, and without relief. Here is a list of things hateful to God. Those sins are in a special manner provoking to God, which are hurtful to the comfort of human life. These things which God hates, we must hate in ourselves; it is nothing to hate them in others. Let us shun all such practices, and watch and pray against them; and avoid, with marked disapproval, all who are guilty of them, whatever may be their rank.

Verses 20-35
The word of God has something to say to us upon all occasions. Let not faithful reproofs ever make us uneasy. When we consider how much this sin abounds, how heinous adultery is in its own nature, of what evil consequence it is, and how certainly it destroys the spiritual life in the soul, we shall not wonder that the cautions against it are so often repeated. Let us notice the subjects of this chapter. Let us remember Him who willingly became our Surety, when we were strangers and enemies. And shall Christians, who have such prospects, motives, and examples, be slothful and careless? Shall we neglect what is pleasing to God, and what he will graciously reward? May we closely watch every sense by which poison can enter our minds or affections.

Keep God's commands close to your heart (verses 1–5)

We must treasure God's commands and guard them carefully.

The instruction is more than “Keep them, and you will live.” We should keep them as people who cannot live without them.

Some people dismiss careful, conscientious obedience as unnecessarily strict.

But God's law is to be guarded like the pupil of the eye.

Indeed, when God's law is written on the heart, it serves as the eye of the soul.

Let the word of God dwell within us and be written where it will always be available for us to read and recall.

In this way we are protected against the destructive effects of our sinful desires and the traps of Satan.

Let God's word strengthen both our fear of sin and our determination to avoid it.

Beware the ways of seducers (verses 6–27)

This passage gives a deeply moving example of the danger of youthful lust.

Whether understood as history or as a parable, it teaches a vital lesson.

After such a vivid account of the danger of approaching sexual temptation, who would dare to place themselves deliberately in its path?

That would resemble a person dancing at the edge of a high cliff immediately after watching someone else fall over it.

Those who bring ruin upon themselves begin by disregarding God's good commands.

We should pray every day that God will keep us from running into temptation.

Otherwise, we virtually invite the enemies of our souls to lay traps for us.

Keep well away from places and situations that encourage vice.

Beware especially of sins advertised as pleasant.

Their apparent attractiveness makes them more dangerous: they readily capture the heart and harden it against repentance.

Consider how an action will end before you begin it.

Even if someone lived as long as Methuselah and spent every day enjoying the greatest pleasures sin could offer, one hour of the anguish and trouble following such a life would outweigh them all.

Christ, God's Wisdom, calls to humanity (verses 1–11)

God makes his will known through creation and human conscience, but more clearly through Moses and the prophets.

The main difficulty is persuading people to pay attention to the instruction they receive.

Yet when even the most ignorant person listens to Christ's words, that teaching can lead to a saving knowledge of the truth.

Where a person has an understanding heart and willingly receives truth with love, wisdom becomes more precious than silver or gold.

The character and riches of Wisdom (verses 12–21)

Here Wisdom is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

He is Christ in the word and Christ in the heart: not only Christ revealed to us, but Christ revealed within us.

Every form of true prudence and ability comes from the Lord.

Through the redemption purchased by Christ's precious blood, the riches of grace overflow in wisdom and good judgment.

Human beings have invented many ways to destroy themselves. God has provided one way to restore us.

Christ hates pride, arrogance, evil conduct and dishonest speech.

These sins make people resistant to his humbling, awakening and holy instruction.

True religion offers the soundest counsel when we face difficult decisions, and helps us see our path clearly.

Christ's wisdom makes those who receive it through love for him genuinely happy.

Seek him early, earnestly and before everything else. Christ has never told anyone to seek him in vain.

People who love him have seen his loveliness and have experienced his love poured into their hearts.

They are blessed here, or in the incomparably better life to come.

Wealth obtained through vanity soon diminishes.

But possessions gained honestly can be put to good use, and what is rightly spent upon godliness and charity has a lasting benefit.

If God's people lack riches and honor in the present world, he will give them something infinitely better.

They enjoy his grace even now.

Through his Spirit, Christ guides them into truth and righteousness; they walk according to the Spirit.

They will also enjoy God's glory hereafter.

Wisdom's promises store up blessings not merely for days or years but for eternity.

That is why her fruit is better than gold.

The eternal Son and the creation of the world (verses 22–31)

In Henry's exposition, the Son of God declares that he was involved in creating the world.

How perfectly suited the Creator of the world is to be its Savior!

Before the world began, the Son was appointed to that great saving work.

If he delights in saving miserable sinners, how could we fail to delight in his salvation?

Hear Christ's voice (verses 32–36)

We should listen to Christ with the readiness of obedient children.

Let us not refuse such mercy.

Blessed are those who hear the Savior's voice and wait upon him through daily Scripture reading, meditation and prayer.

People devoted to the world make time for empty amusements while still attending to what they regard as essential.

When professing believers seek excuses to neglect the means of grace, do they not show contempt for Wisdom's instruction?

Christ is both Wisdom and Life to everyone who believes.

We cannot obtain God's favor unless we find Christ and are found in him.

Those who offend Christ injure their own souls.

Sinners are destroyed because they choose the way of destruction.

God therefore remains just when he judges them.

Wisdom invites people to Christ (verses 1–12)

Christ has prepared ordinances through which those who believe receive spiritual nourishment in this life, and dwelling places in heaven where they will be received afterward.

Ministers of the gospel go out to invite guests to this feast.

The invitation is open to everyone; it excludes no one except those who refuse to come.

Our Savior came not to call people who consider themselves righteous, but sinners.

He did not come to call those who are wise in their own eyes and think they already see clearly.

We must leave the companionship and foolish pleasures of ungodly people if we are to enjoy the pleasures of a holy life.

Seeking out the company of wicked people in the confident expectation of doing them good is dangerous: we are often more likely to be corrupted by them.

It is not enough to abandon the foolish; we must join those who walk in wisdom.

True wisdom is found in the way of godliness, and true life lies at the end of that way.

Those who embrace it are blessed.

We cannot add anything to God's own happiness or profit him through our obedience. The benefit is ours, not his.

But consider the disgrace and destruction awaiting those who disregard Wisdom's invitation.

God is not the author of sin.

Satan can tempt, but he cannot force anyone to sin.

Those who scorn this offer must bear the loss of what they have rejected. Their contempt makes their condemnation greater.

Folly offers a deceptive invitation (verses 13–18)

See how diligently the tempter works to draw unwary people into sin.

Worldly and sensual pleasures dull the conscience and extinguish the first sparks of conviction.

Folly cannot offer sound reasons for following her.

When she rules a person's soul, knowledge of holy things is forgotten and lost.

Her invitations are persistent and demanding.

We need to seek true wisdom and pray for it, because Satan has many ways of drawing our souls away from Christ.

Not only bodily lusts and openly wicked seducers endanger people.

False teachers also lead thousands toward destruction with doctrines that flatter pride and grant permission to sinful desire.

They are especially dangerous to people whose first serious concern for their souls has not yet taken deep root.

Satan's depths are the depths of hell.

Unrepented sin ends in destruction without remedy.

Solomon shows us the hook hidden beneath the bait. Those who believe his warning will not reach for it.

Notice how miserable, empty, unsatisfying and deceptive are the pleasures sin offers, even when they seem to have been stolen for our enjoyment.

May our desire for the eternal enjoyment of Jesus Christ become so strong that we live by faith for him each day now and soon live with him in glory.

Original chapter-level introductory comment

Throughout Proverbs, we should look for a meaning beyond each passage's first and most immediate application. Henry sees that deeper meaning in Jesus Christ, the Wisdom so often spoken of throughout this book.

Verse 1 — Children and their parents

Parents' happiness depends greatly upon their children. This gives children and parents alike strong reasons to fulfill their duties faithfully.

Verses 2 and 3 — The soul's real needs

A righteous person may be poor, but the Lord will not let that person lack what is necessary for spiritual life.

Verse 4 — Diligence in the Lord's service

People who are fervent in spirit, serving the Lord are likely to become rich in faith and good works.

Verse 5 — Use opportunities wisely

Those who waste their opportunities deserve rebuke, for they are neglecting chances to prepare both for this life and the life to come.

Verse 6 — True blessing

The blessings resting upon faithful people are not empty appearances: they are real blessings.

Verse 7 — The difference that outlasts death

Both righteous and wicked people must die, but their souls face vastly different conditions.

Verse 8 — Wisdom put into practice

A person who is wise in heart acts upon the knowledge received.

Verse 9 — The exposure of deceit

People who disguise their intentions and continually evade the truth will eventually be found out.

Verse 10 — Craftiness does not excuse sin

Cleverness and cunning cannot make wrongdoing innocent.

Verse 11 — Words that bring life

A good person speaks to teach, encourage and correct others.

Verse 12 — Love maintains peace

Where hatred rules, every small event produces quarrels. By patiently bearing with one another, we preserve peace and harmony.

Verse 13 — Foolishness invites correction

Those who persist foolishly in wicked ways are preparing their own punishment.

Verse 14 — Store up useful knowledge

We should treasure all knowledge that may be useful, so it will be ready when we need it. We gain this wisdom through reading, listening to God's word, meditation, prayer and faith in Christ, whom God makes wisdom for us.

Verse 15 — The mistaken confidence of rich and poor

Both rich and poor people may misunderstand their material circumstances. Wealth can expose people to many dangers. Someone with little may nevertheless live comfortably with contentment, a good conscience and faith.

Verse 16 — Work that leads to life

A righteous person may own nothing beyond what hard work produces. Yet that labor leads to life.

Verse 17 — Receive correction

A traveler who has lost the way and refuses directions toward the right road will remain lost.

Verse 18 — Nothing can be hidden from God

It is especially foolish to imagine anything can be concealed from God. Malice is no less evil.

Verse 19 — Restrain excessive speech

Those who speak too much often say many things they should not. Restraining our words is wisdom and helps preserve our peace.

Verses 20 and 21 — The words of the righteous

The speech of the righteous is sincere, free from the impurities of deceit and evil design. Godly conversation becomes spiritual nourishment for people in need. Foolish people perish because they lack heart or thoughtful understanding, as the Hebrew expression indicates.

Verse 22 — Wealth without sorrow

The truly desirable kind of wealth brings neither anguish in enjoying it, despair when it is lost, nor guilt through misuse. What comes from God's love is accompanied by God's grace.

Verse 23 — Harm is no game

Only the foolish and wicked take pleasure in harming others or enticing them into sin.

Verse 24 — The hope of the righteous

The righteous person's greatest desire for eternal blessings will be fulfilled.

Verse 25 — The brief prosperity of sinners

The apparent success of unrepentant sinners resembles a whirlwind: it soon exhausts itself and vanishes.

Verse 26 — A lazy worker brings distress

Just as vinegar irritates the teeth and smoke stings the eyes, a lazy person causes frustration and trouble to an employer.

Verses 27 and 28 — Reverence and lasting hope

Who desires life? Fear God. He gives his people all the life necessary in this world and eternal life in the next. Their hope is therefore lasting.

Verse 29 — The believer grows stronger

Those who trust God increase in faith, and obedience becomes increasingly delightful to them.

Verse 30 — Earth is not the wicked person's permanent home

Wicked people might wish to remain on earth among their idols forever, but they cannot. They must die and leave those idols behind.

Verses 31 and 32 — Speech that benefits others

A good person speaks with wisdom for other people's benefit. The wicked speak things displeasing to God and offensive to those around them; this is both their sin and their ruin. The righteous are preserved by God's power, and nothing can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.
